client: I’ve been really stressed since I lost my job back in February. I keep worrying about money and whether I’ll find something that pays enough to cover my bills. Every time I try to update my resume, I feel stuck—like I don’t even know where to start or how to make myself stand out. Honestly, I’m not sure if talking about it will really help me figure this out.
therapist: It sounds like losing your job has brought up a lot of uncertainty and worry, especially around finances and the job search process—those feelings are completely valid given the situation. When you try to update your resume, what thoughts come up that make you feel stuck?

client: I just keep thinking that my skills aren’t good enough, or that no one will want to hire me because I’ve been out of work for a while. It feels like I’m competing with people who are way more qualified, and I don’t measure up. I know I should try, but it’s hard to motivate myself when I feel like it’s pointless.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught in a cycle of self-doubt, which can make taking those first steps feel overwhelming. Have you ever considered exploring what evidence supports or challenges the thought that your skills aren’t good enough? Sometimes breaking it down can help shift perspective.

client: I guess I haven’t really thought about it that way, but I’m not sure if looking for evidence will help. It feels like the proof is right there—I didn’t get hired in the last few interviews I went to, so doesn’t that mean my skills aren’t enough? It’s hard to argue with that.
therapist: I hear how those past interviews have reinforced this belief about your skills, and rejection can feel very personal. Might there be other factors—like the job market or company needs—that played a role, rather than it being solely about your abilities?

client: I never really considered that—I always took it as me not being good enough. I mean, one of the jobs I interviewed for did get canceled because of budget cuts... but it's hard not to blame myself. Even if there are other reasons, what if I'm just making excuses?
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of self-blame, even when external factors, like budget cuts, were clearly out of your control. How might it feel to explore whether your self-criticism might be outweighing the actual circumstances?

client: I guess I do tend to assume the worst about myself. But even if I try to see it differently, it’s hard to shake the feeling that I should’ve done something more—prepared better, networked more, whatever. Like maybe if I’d tried harder, I wouldn’t be in this situation now.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding yourself to an impossibly high standard—as if there was some perfect amount of effort that could have prevented this situation entirely. What might it feel like to treat yourself with the same compassion you'd offer a friend going through this?

client: If it were a friend, I’d probably tell them they’re being too hard on themselves and that it’s not their fault. But for some reason, I can’t seem to apply that to myself. It feels like if I’m too compassionate, I’ll just let myself off the hook and stop trying altogether. I don’t know how to balance being kind to myself with staying motivated.
therapist: It sounds like you’re worried that self-compassion might lead to complacency, but in reality, being kind to yourself can actually help you approach challenges with more clarity and energy. What might it feel like to experiment with treating yourself with the same understanding you’d offer a friend, while still holding onto your motivation?

client: I’m not sure if I can separate self-compassion from feeling like I’m letting myself off the hook. It’s like I’ve always pushed myself hard to get things done, and if I stop doing that, I’m afraid I’ll just give up. I don’t know how to balance being kind to myself and still feeling like I’m working hard enough.
therapist: It sounds like you’ve always relied on self-criticism as a way to motivate yourself, and the idea of letting go of that feels scary—like you might lose your drive. What if self-compassion could actually help you approach tasks with less pressure, making it easier to take action without feeling overwhelmed? How might it feel to explore small, manageable steps forward while practicing kindness toward yourself?

client: I guess I’ve never thought about self-compassion as a way to actually help me move forward—it always felt like it would just make me lazy. But the idea of taking small steps feels a little less overwhelming than trying to tackle everything at once. I’m just not sure how to start being kind to myself when I’m so used to being hard on myself. It feels unnatural, like I’m forcing it.
therapist: It’s completely understandable that self-compassion feels unnatural when you’re so used to pushing yourself through criticism—it’s like learning a new skill, and it takes time to feel comfortable. What might it feel like to start small, like acknowledging one thing you’re doing well each day, even if it feels a bit forced at first?

client: Acknowledging one thing I’m doing well each day... I guess I could try, but it feels a bit forced, like I’m just pretending. And what if I can’t even think of anything? I’m just not used to focusing on positives—it feels easier to notice where I’m falling short. I’m worried I’ll just end up feeling fake or frustrated with myself.
therapist: It sounds like the idea of focusing on positives feels unfamiliar and even uncomfortable, which is completely valid—it’s hard to shift a mindset you’ve relied on for so long. What if you started with something small, like noticing a moment when you took a step forward, no matter how tiny, and simply acknowledging it without judgment? How might that feel?

client: I guess I could try noticing small steps, like updating my resume or sending out an application, even if it feels like such a small thing. But I’m worried I’ll just brush it off as not being enough—like it doesn’t really count unless it leads to something big, like getting an interview or a job offer. It’s hard to feel like those small steps matter.
therapist: It sounds like you're measuring progress only by big outcomes, which can make the smaller but important steps feel invisible. What if you tried to recognize that every action—no matter how small—is part of building momentum, even if the results aren’t immediate? How might it feel to acknowledge that effort as valuable in itself?
